The best LLM tools in 2026 are LangChain and LlamaIndex for building the application, OpenRouter and LiteLLM for reaching hundreds of models through one API, and LangSmith or Langfuse for seeing what your app actually did in production. Hugging Face, the Vercel AI SDK, Weights & Biases (now part of CoreWeave Forge), and Simon Willison's llm CLI round out the list of 10.

This guide is a map of the whole LLM developer stack, with one short list per layer. It is not about running models on your own hardware: our best local LLM tools guide covers Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, and llama.cpp. It is also not a deep ranking of runtimes and gateways for enterprise teams; if you are choosing between LangGraph, Portkey, Kong, and 11 other orchestration layers, read our enterprise LLM orchestration tools ranking instead. Use this page to decide which layers you need, then go deep where it matters.
Every price, license, and GitHub star count below was checked against the vendor's own site, pricing page, or repository on October 21, 2026.
TL;DR: the 10 LLM tools, by layer
To build: LangChain for agents, tool-calling, and integrations; LlamaIndex for connecting a model to your documents; the Vercel AI SDK for TypeScript and Next.js teams.

To reach models: Hugging Face for open models and datasets; OpenRouter for one hosted API across 468 models with no markup on inference; LiteLLM for the same unified API self-hosted on your own infrastructure.
To trace and evaluate: LangSmith if you are on LangChain or LangGraph; Langfuse if you want open source and self-hosting; Weights & Biases if your team already tracks training runs there.
To test prompts: llm, a command-line tool for running prompts against any provider from a terminal.

Build: frameworks that turn an API call into an application

This is the layer that turns "call a model" into "an application with memory, tools, and retrieval." If your decision is specifically which agent framework to standardize on, the orchestration ranking linked above goes further than this section does.
1. LangChain, best for agents and broad integrations

LangChain is the framework most teams mean when they say they are "building on an LLM." It handles tool-calling, memory, structured output, and a large library of integrations for vector stores, APIs, and data sources. Its GitHub description now reads "The agent engineering platform," and the Python package is on version 1.4.6 as of October 2026. The repository has about 148,000 stars under the MIT license.

LangGraph, from the same team, is the lower-level graph runtime (about 43,600 stars, MIT) for when you need explicit control over state, branching, and retries instead of LangChain's higher-level agent abstractions.
Pricing. The framework is free. LangSmith, the company's paid observability product, is covered below.
Best for. Python teams building agents that call tools and need a ready-made integration for most of their stack.
Watch out for. The abstraction layer adds indirection you have to learn and debug through. Small single-provider apps often need less than LangChain gives you.
2. LlamaIndex, best for connecting a model to your documents

LlamaIndex is the framework people reach for when the job is retrieval-augmented generation: indexing your documents and data so the model answers from them instead of from its training set. The open-source core (llama-index, MIT) handles ingestion, indexing, retrieval, and query pipelines, and the project's README lists over 300 integration packages for LLMs, embedding models, and vector stores.

One change matters for anyone choosing it in late 2026. The README now states that the company's "primary focus has shifted towards LlamaParse," its commercial platform for agentic OCR, parsing, and extraction, while the open-source framework remains "available as an open toolkit." The framework still ships releases (version 0.14.25 in October 2026), but expect the company's new investment to land in LlamaParse first.

Pricing. The framework is free. LlamaParse has a Free plan with 10K credits, Starter at $50/month (40K credits), Pro at $500/month (400K credits), and custom Enterprise pricing, with 1,000 credits priced at $1.25.
Best for. Teams whose hard problem is messy documents (PDFs, scans, tables) rather than agent logic.
Watch out for. The shifted company focus. If you need a long-lived RAG framework, compare it with Haystack and LangChain's own retrieval tooling before committing.
3. Vercel AI SDK, best for TypeScript and Next.js teams

The Vercel AI SDK is a TypeScript toolkit for building LLM features and agents, made by the team behind Next.js. Where LangChain and LlamaIndex are Python-first, the AI SDK gives TypeScript teams one API for text generation, structured output, tool calls, and agents, plus UI hooks for chat interfaces. It is on major version 7 (ai 7.0.148 on npm), has about 27,400 GitHub stars, and is licensed Apache 2.0. Official providers include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Groq, DeepSeek, xAI, and others, with more available as community providers.
Pricing. The SDK is free. Hosting on Vercel is a separate product, and the SDK works the same wherever you deploy.
Best for. Teams already on React or Next.js that want streaming chat and tool-calling without adopting a Python-oriented framework.
Watch out for. A smaller integration catalog than LangChain for retrieval and data connectors, so RAG-heavy apps often pair it with a separate retrieval layer.

Access: models, hubs, and routing
4. Hugging Face, best for finding and hosting open models

Hugging Face is where open models, datasets, and demo apps (Spaces) live. Nearly every open-weight release is published or mirrored there, and its transformers library has about 168,000 GitHub stars under Apache 2.0.

Pricing. The public hub is free. PRO is $9/month for individuals, Team is $20/user/month, and Enterprise is $50/user/month. Compute is metered separately: basic CPU Spaces are free, upgraded CPU is $0.03/hour, an NVIDIA T4 Space starts at $0.40/hour, and Inference Endpoints start at $0.033/hour.
Best for. Teams that need to find, fine-tune, or host an open model, or put a demo online without their own infrastructure.
Watch out for. If your stack only calls closed hosted models, you may not need Hugging Face at all.
5. OpenRouter, best for one hosted API across many providers

OpenRouter gives you one API key and one request format that routes to whichever model you name. Its public models API listed 468 models on October 21, 2026, and its pricing page states that inference is billed at each provider's list price on every plan, so there is no markup on tokens.

Pricing. The fee sits on credit purchases instead: 5.5% on the Standard plan and 8% on Business, with discounted Enterprise contracts. If you bring your own provider keys (BYOK), the first $25,000 of list-price inference per month carries no fee, and usage above that costs 5% of what the same request would cost through OpenRouter.
Best for. Teams that want to A/B test models across providers or keep a fallback path ready for provider outages.
Watch out for. Every request passes through a third party, which some compliance reviews will not accept.
6. LiteLLM, best for a self-hosted gateway you control

LiteLLM is the self-hosted counterpart to OpenRouter: an open-source AI gateway and Python SDK that calls 100+ LLM providers in the OpenAI request format, with virtual keys, budgets, and cost tracking. It has about 61,700 GitHub stars. Code outside its enterprise/ directory is MIT-licensed, and a license key adds enterprise features: SSO, SCIM, audit logs of admin changes, and per-team admins. A Rust gateway is listed as a beta product.
Pricing. Free to self-host; you pay only for your infrastructure and provider tokens. Enterprise pricing is not published (a 30-day trial is offered, then "talk to sales").
Best for. Teams that need every LLM request to stay on infrastructure they control, for compliance, latency, or cost reasons.
Watch out for. You run it. Upgrades, uptime, and scaling are your team's job, not a vendor's.
Observe: tracing and evaluation

Once an LLM app is live, the question changes from "does the demo work" to "what did it do for this user, and was the answer right." Our AI agent observability tools guide compares 12 options in depth; these are the three most teams shortlist first.
7. LangSmith, best if you build on LangChain or LangGraph

LangSmith is LangChain's commercial platform for tracing, debugging, and evaluating LLM apps, and it works whether or not the app uses LangChain. It records every step of a run, including prompts, tool calls, and outputs, and layers evaluation datasets and automated grading on top.

Pricing. Developer is $0 for one seat with 5K base traces per month. Plus is $39 per seat per month with 10K base traces and access to Deployment. Enterprise is custom and adds self-hosted or hybrid options. Traces beyond the allowance are pay as you go; base traces keep 14 days of retention and extended traces keep 180 days. Some features bill in LangChain Standard Units at $1.00 each.
Best for. Teams on LangChain or LangGraph that want the tightest integration from the same company.
Watch out for. Your bill scales with trace volume as well as seats, so model expected traffic before you budget.
8. Langfuse, best open-source option you can self-host

Langfuse is an open-source platform for tracing, evaluations, prompt management, and a playground. ClickHouse acquired it in January 2026, and Langfuse said at the time that it would stay open source and self-hostable with no planned licensing changes. The repository has about 36,100 stars; code outside its ee directories is MIT-licensed. Its README lists integrations with LangChain, LlamaIndex, LiteLLM, the OpenAI SDK, and the Vercel AI SDK.

Pricing (cloud). Hobby is free with 50K units per month. Core is $29/month with 100K units, Pro is $199/month with three years of data access, and Enterprise is $2,499/month. Overage on paid plans is $8 per 100K units, dropping at higher volumes. Self-hosting is free.
Best for. Teams with a self-hosting requirement or that want to avoid per-unit cloud billing.
Watch out for. Self-hosting means running the stack (including its databases) yourself.
9. Weights & Biases, best if your team already tracks training runs there

Weights & Biases (W&B) began as an experiment tracker for model training and added LLM tracing and evaluation through its Weave toolkit. CoreWeave completed its acquisition of W&B in May 2025, and as of September 30, 2026, W&B is part of CoreWeave Forge: Free, Pro, and Enterprise SaaS accounts now sign in through Forge with their existing credentials, and accounts, projects, and API keys stay the same. The wandb client is MIT-licensed with about 11,300 GitHub stars.
Pricing. Free ($0, up to 5 model seats, 1 GB/month of Weave ingestion). Pro starts at $60/month billed monthly, with a 30-day trial, and is aimed at teams under 50 employees. Enterprise is custom.
Best for. ML teams that fine-tune or train models in W&B and want LLM app evaluation in the same place.
Watch out for. The Forge transition is recent, so expect plan names and pages to keep moving for a while.
Test: prompt tooling
10. llm (Simon Willison), best for testing prompts from a terminal

llm is a command-line tool and Python library by Simon Willison for running prompts against hosted and local models without writing a script first. Plugins add providers (for example llm-anthropic, llm-gemini, and llm-ollama), every prompt and response is logged to a local SQLite database, and models can be given tools. It is on version 0.36, licensed Apache 2.0, with about 12,600 GitHub stars.
Pricing. Free; you pay only the providers you call.
Best for. Developers comparing providers or scripting a one-off LLM task before building an app around it.
Watch out for. It is a developer tool, not a production runtime or a team platform.

How to choose the right LLM tools for your stack

Most production LLM apps need one tool from each of three layers: a framework to build with, an access layer to reach models, and an observability tool to see what happened. Work through these questions in order.
1) Which language is your team building in?

Pick the framework that matches your codebase. Python teams usually start with LangChain (or LangGraph for explicit control) and add LlamaIndex when document retrieval is the core job. TypeScript and Next.js teams get a lighter path with the Vercel AI SDK.
2) Can your requests go through a third party?

If yes, OpenRouter is the fastest route to many providers with no token markup. If compliance or data residency rules that out, run LiteLLM on your own infrastructure. If you mostly use open weights, Hugging Face is where you will find and host them.
3) Do you need to self-host your traces?

If traces can live in a vendor cloud and you are on LangChain, LangSmith is the shortest setup. If they must stay in-house, Langfuse self-hosts for free. If your ML team already lives in W&B, add Weave there instead of adopting a second platform.
4) What will it cost at your real volume?

Total cost is mostly tokens and trace volume, not seat prices. Run a two-week pilot on real traffic, then price LangSmith traces, Langfuse units, and OpenRouter credit fees against what you actually logged.

Choosing tools gets you the parts. Connecting them to your data, your systems, and a permission model that gives an agent only the access it needs is where most of the engineering time goes. FAQ
What are the best LLM tools in 2026?

The best LLM tools in 2026 are LangChain, LlamaIndex, and the Vercel AI SDK for building apps; Hugging Face, OpenRouter, and LiteLLM for model access; LangSmith, Langfuse, and Weights & Biases for tracing and evaluation; and Simon Willison's llm CLI for testing prompts. Most teams need one tool from the build, access, and observe layers, not all ten.
What counts as an LLM tool?

An LLM tool is software for building, connecting to, or monitoring applications that use large language models. In this guide that means frameworks, model access layers, observability platforms, and prompt tooling. Software for running models on your own hardware is a separate category, covered in our local LLM tools guide.
What is the difference between LangChain and LlamaIndex?

LangChain is a general framework for agents, tool-calling, and integrations, while LlamaIndex focuses on connecting a model to your documents and data for retrieval. Many projects use both: LangChain or LangGraph for the application logic and LlamaIndex for retrieval. Note that LlamaIndex the company now puts its main focus on its commercial LlamaParse platform.
Is LangChain free?

Yes, the LangChain framework is free and MIT-licensed. LangSmith, the company's observability product, has a free Developer plan for one seat with 5K base traces per month, and a Plus plan at $39 per seat per month plus usage.
Does OpenRouter charge more than going direct to a provider?

No, OpenRouter bills inference at each provider's list price with no markup. Its fees sit elsewhere: 5.5% on credit purchases on the Standard plan (8% on Business), and 5% on bring-your-own-key usage above a free $25,000 of list-price inference per month.
What is the difference between OpenRouter and LiteLLM?

OpenRouter is a hosted service you call over its API, while LiteLLM is an open-source gateway you run yourself. Both give you one interface across many providers. Pick OpenRouter to avoid managing infrastructure, and LiteLLM when every request must stay on systems you control.
